The seven-fingered threadfin, Filimanus heptadactyla, is a coastal species found throughout the Indo-West Pacific region, where it inhabits shallow sandy and muddy substrates. Field surveys indicate that this fish attains a maximum total length of 38 centimeters [Li = 38 centimeters], a size that places it among the medium-sized members of the family Polynemidae. The species is characterized by its elongated body and the distinctive seven pectoral filaments that give it its common name, with these filamentous rays being notably longer in mature individuals. Growth rates vary considerably across its range, influenced by local water temperatures and food availability. In populations from the Gulf of Thailand, individuals frequently reach total lengths exceeding 30 centimeters within their third year, though the asymptotic length appears to be set at this 38 centimeter [Li = 38 centimeter] maximum across most studied locations. Lunar phase and tidal cycles strongly influence foraging behavior, with adults moving into intertidal zones during flood tides to prey on small crustaceans and polychaetes. The species is frequently taken as bycatch in artisanal trawl fisheries, where its flesh is considered of moderate quality for human consumption.

Reproductive biology in Filimanus heptadactyla follows a pattern typical of many tropical polynemids, with spawning occurring throughout much of the year in warmer waters. Marked gonadal development becomes evident when individuals attain a total length of approximately 19 centimeters [Lp = approximately 19 centimeters], which corresponds to the onset of sexual maturation. At this size, the gonadosomatic index rises sharply, signaling the transition from the juvenile to the adult reproductive phase. Histological examination of ovarian tissue reveals asynchronous oocyte development, indicating that this species is a batch spawner capable of releasing multiple clutches over an extended breeding season. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 27 °C [T = 27 °C], researchers recorded that reproductively active females produce an average of approximately 10 oocytes per day [Ri = approximately 10 oocytes per day], a rate derived from the product of clutch size and clutch frequency.

The earliest life stages of the seven-fingered threadfin are characterized by a heavy reliance on endogenous yolk reserves. Fertilized eggs, which are pelagic and spherical, measure approximately 0.775 millimeters in diameter. Upon hatching, the prolarvae emerge with a wet weight at birth of just 0.00024 grams [Wwb = 0.00024 grams], a diminutive size that reflects the modest energy reserves packaged within the fertilized ovum. During the yolk-sac larval phase, which lasts roughly three to four days depending on ambient temperature, the larvae subsist entirely on their endogenous yolk stores before transitioning to exogenous feeding. First feeding typically commences following mouth opening and retinal differentiation, at which point the larvae begin to capture small copepod nauplii and rotifers. The exotrophic transition is a critical period of high mortality, with larval survival rates strongly tied to the availability of appropriate prey items in the plankton. Field collections of ichthyoplankton suggest that larval abundance peaks during the monsoon season, when nutrient runoff fuels elevated primary and secondary productivity in nearshore waters, thereby enhancing food resources for these tiny, actively growing larvae.

As individuals progress through the juvenile and sub-adult stages, body mass increases substantially, with the asymptotic wet weight being attained in older, fully mature specimens. Sexual maturity, however, is reached at a considerably lower body mass; field-caught individuals undergoing first vitellogenesis or spermatogenesis typically weigh approximately 60.4 grams [Wwp = approximately 60.4 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions of collected specimens. This mass corresponds closely to the 19 centimeter total length threshold for pubertal onset noted earlier. Continued growth beyond this point is fueled by a diet increasingly dominated by larger benthic invertebrates such as penaeid shrimps and small crabs. The ultimate wet weight recorded for this species is 515 grams [Wwi = 515 grams], a value representing the maximum body mass achieved by the largest individuals observed in the wild. This substantial increase from the pubertal weight to the ultimate weight underscores the considerable energetic investment the species makes in somatic growth before and during its reproductive lifespan. Body condition indices vary seasonally, with peak values typically recorded just prior to the main rainy season, when prey resources are most abundant.

Longevity in Filimanus heptadactyla has been assessed through both captive rearing studies and analysis of otolith daily increments from wild-caught specimens. Under natural thermal regimes characteristic of its tropical range at a mean annual water temperature of 29 °C [T = 29 °C] the species exhibits a maximum documented lifespan of 3,650 days [am = 3,650 days], equivalent to a 10-year longevity (10 years) [am = 10 years]. This relatively extended lifespan for a medium-sized coastal fish likely reflects the species' iteroparous breeding strategy, which distributes reproductive effort across multiple seasons and thereby reduces the physiological stress of a single, high-cost spawning event. Age-structured population models suggest that natural mortality rates are moderate, with the highest mortality occurring during the first year of life due to predation on eggs and larvae. The combination of a 10-year lifespan and batch spawning behavior enables the species to buffer against years of poor recruitment, a demographic advantage in the unpredictable shallow-water habitats it frequents. Senescence in older adults is accompanied by a gradual decline in gonadal output and a reduction in the condition factor, marking the terminal phase of the life cycle.
